On 2023-05-30, the user shared Next.js documentation about Route Handlers and received an overview. Route Handlers are request handlers defined in route.js or route.ts files inside the app directory, use Web Request/Response APIs (with NextRequest and NextResponse helpers), and support GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, and OPTIONS. They cannot occupy the same route segment as a page.js file and do not participate in layouts or client-side navigation. GET handlers using Response can be statically evaluated by default; using a Request parameter, other HTTP methods, or dynamic functions such as cookies and headers makes handlers dynamic. The documentation covered revalidation, cookies and headers, redirects, dynamic segments, streaming, request bodies, Edge and Node.js runtimes, and returning files such as robots.txt, rss.xml, and sitemap.xml. It noted that generateStaticParams() was not supported for Route Handlers.

records.text: The chapter described Bai et al. (2019), “Wearable Travel Aid for Environment Perception and Navigation of Visually Impaired People”: a consumer RGB-D camera mounted on eyeglasses, an IMU attached to the camera, a smartphone for detection and routing, and an earphone for spoken feedback. The system is intended for indoor and outdoor use and uses computer vision as a lightweight, low-cost alternative to sensors such as ultrasonic and LiDAR. Limitations: weak detection of small obstacles and no staircase detection.
entities: Wearable Travel Aid for Environment Perception and Navigation of Visually Impaired People

records.text: The chapter described Jiang et al. (2016), “Let Blind People See: Real-Time Visual Recognition with Results Converted to 3D Audio”: video from a portable camera is streamed to a server for real-time YOLO recognition; object bounding-box location and size are used to derive 3D location, and Unity sends spatial audio through wireless earphones. The described system achieved 30 frames per second at 1080p. Limitations: accurate object detection and classification only within 2–5 metres, earbuds block ambient sound, and multiple detected objects can overwhelm the user with information.
entities: Let Blind People See: Real-Time Visual Recognition with Results Converted to 3D Audio

records.text: The chapter described Bharatia et al. (2019), “Smart Electronic Stick for Visually Impaired using Android Application and Google’s Cloud Vision”: an Android voice-controlled application works with a lightweight electronic stick. Ultrasonic sensors detect low-lying and knee-level obstacles and potholes when moving backwards, with buzzer alerts. Other described capabilities include Bluetooth-connected GPS navigation, sharing a user's live location with family or a nearby help centre in emergencies, face detection, Cloud Vision interpretation of traffic lights and roadside signs, text recognition from photos, stick tracking, NLP voice commands, and rechargeable circuitry. The stated limitations are short obstacle-detection coverage and suitability only for indoor use.
entities: Smart Electronic Stick for Visually Impaired using Android Application and Google’s Cloud Vision

records.text: The chapter described WeWalk, a smart cane developed by the nonprofit YGA. Its traditional-looking cane has a touchpad, an above-ground ultrasonic sensor, vibration or audio obstacle alerts, and Bluetooth pairing with a phone. Its application supports accessible mapping, place discovery and navigation, transit information such as nearby bus stops and timetables, and voice assistance; the cane or phone can play a sound to help locate it if lost. Stated limitations: the cane costs USD 500, rain or snow may cause cane or speaker malfunction, and the cane tip is loud on rough sidewalks.
entities: WeWALK Smart Cane – Smart Cane for the Visually Impaired (2020)

records.text: The chapter described Asati et al. (2019), “Development of an Intelligent Cane for Visually Impaired Human Subjects”: an intelligent white cane uses HR-SO4 ultrasonic sensors to detect and measure the distance of obstacles, including above-head-level objects; warnings are delivered as buzzer beeps. A webcam captures images for object classification, which is converted into text and audio using text-to-speech. The chapter states a sensor range of 450 metres. Limitations: high system-building cost, inability to identify potholes, and detection in rainy weather was not tested.
entities: Development of an Intelligent Cane for Visually Impaired Human Subjects

records.text: The chapter described Dosi et al. (2018), “Android Application for Object Recognition Using Neural Networks for the Visually Impaired”: an Android application uses the phone camera and a convolutional neural network based on MobileNets for real-time object recognition, then speaks the recognized object. Limitations: it works only offline; unknown or untrained objects are predicted using existing database images; and the model must be retrained to recognize untrained objects.
entities: Android Application for Object Recognition Using Neural Networks for the Visually Impaired

records.text: The chapter described Duman et al. (2019), “Design and Implementation of an Embedded Real-Time System for Guiding Visually Impaired Individuals”: a handheld Raspberry Pi camera captures footage, and YOLO on a Raspberry Pi detects objects. For detected people, bounding-box size is used to estimate distance; the reported distance-estimation accuracy is 98.8%. Temporary text results, including object labels and estimated human distance, are converted to audio alerts played at intervals to reduce noise and ambiguity. Limitations: the system detects only humans and has no wearable design.
entities: Design and Implementation of an Embedded Real-Time System for Guiding Visually Impaired Individuals

records.text: The chapter described Anish Aralikatti et al. (2020), “Real-time object detection and face recognition system to assist the visually impaired”: an Android phone application uses its camera, OpenCV, Tiny YOLO for object and human detection, and FaceNet for face identification; detections are presented to the user as audio. The stated limitation is lower accuracy than YOLO because Tiny YOLO is a smaller model.
entities: Real-time object detection and face recognition system to assist the visually impaired
